metadata.title: Cross-cultural differential item functioning in the PISA 2022 creative thinking assessment

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses secondary microdata from the OECD PISA 2022 Creative Thinking (CT) international database, combining the CT cognitive item-response file with the student background questionnaire file. The analysis is conducted via an IRT-based multi-group DFIT procedure across ten cultural clusters, with separate cluster calibrations and subsequent scale linking (Stocking–Lord TCC) and anchor purification. The manuscript does not report the use of PISA complex survey sampling weights (e.g., student design weights) or replicate-weight procedures, and it does not name any weight variable. Given the focus on item/test differential functioning and the use of large-sample IRT calibration, the weighting strategy is unclear; readers should treat the DIF indices as conditional on the modeling approach rather than as explicitly population-representative estimates unless weights are confirmed in the OSF script.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This study does not use PV-based achievement scores as the dependent variable; instead, it applies an IRT-based DFIT framework to scored CT item responses and estimates group-specific item parameters and expected item scores on a latent creative thinking proficiency scale. Because the analysis is based on IRT calibration with missing responses treated as missing at random, the paper does not describe a PV-specific plausible-values workflow. As a result, PV handling is not applicable to the DIF estimation, and the paper does not provide a separate, explicit missing-data handling strategy for PVs.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analytic sample includes all PISA 2022 Creative Thinking (CT) students who provided at least five valid responses to a CT item, to ensure stable ability estimation and avoid excessively noisy θ estimates. For the DIF calibration, the initial CT item pool comprised 32 scored open-ended tasks; two tasks were excluded because at least one cultural cluster showed complete non-response, preventing stable parameter estimation in those groups. The final analytic set for DFIT consisted of 30 items. Cultural clustering was implemented by assigning each participating economy to one of ten extended GLOBE clusters (Mensah & Chen), and DIF comparisons were conducted using a pairwise contrast design with the Anglo cluster (CLUID = 2) as the fixed reference group.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2022 Creative Thinking (CT) Grade 10/15-year-olds, cross-cultural DIF (IRT-DFIT) across cultural clusters
main_findings.target_variable: Item-level differential functioning (NCDIF; DIF flagging across cultural clusters)
main_findings.performance_metrics: DFIT results: 25 of 30 items flagged for DIF (83.3%); 5 items showed no DIF (16.7%). DIF magnitude threshold: NCDIF > 0.0115. Largest item-level effects reported: DT360Q01C2 (Max NCDIF = 0.188) and DT500Q01C (Max NCDIF = 0.176). Additional analysis (Cluster-level DIF disadvantage (signed area SA and test-level DIF index DTF vs Anglo)): Cluster-level summary (Table 3): Sub-Saharan Africa—16 DIF items, 11 disadvantaging (SA < 0), net mean SA = −0.690, DTF = 1.668, peak disadvantage item DT500Q01C (SA = −2.642). Germanic Europe—8 DIF items, 8 disadvantaging, net mean SA = −0.819, DTF = 2.485, peak disadvantage item DT360Q01C2 (SA = −1.200). Confucian Asia—14 DIF items, 3 disadvantaging, net mean SA = 0.338, DTF = 3.944 (net advantage). Nordic Europe—4 DIF items, 1 disadvantaging, net mean SA = 0.475, DTF = 0.873.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 Creative Thinking (CT) the study leveraged cultural cluster membership to evaluate item-level differential functioning (NCDIF) across groups, finding that 83.3% of CT items showed DIF above the practical threshold (NCDIF > 0.0115) while 16.7% were invariant. This indicates that cross-cultural comparability in creative thinking is threatened by widespread but mostly modest item non-equivalence, implying that OECD/PISA should treat DIF monitoring as a routine quality assurance step for open-ended creativity tasks, not only for traditional domains.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2022 Creative Thinking (CT) Grade 10/15-year-olds, qualitative diagnosis of DIF items
main_findings.target_variable: Mechanisms explaining DIF (four interpretive dimensions applied to high-impact items)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Qualitative case focus on two high-impact publicly documented items: DT500Q01C (peak disadvantage for Sub-Saharan Africa; SA = −2.642) and DT240Q02C (peak disadvantage for Middle East; SA = −1.968). Mechanisms mapped to four dimensions: (1) context familiarity, (2) scenario-activated cognitive prototypes, (3) embedded value assumptions, (4) response-mode alignment.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 Creative Thinking (CT) the study leveraged cultural-cluster DIF flags to select high-impact items and then used a four-dimension qualitative framework to explain why DIF emerges, finding that culturally unfamiliar contexts, culturally different problem scripts, rubric value asymmetries, and response-mode misalignment jointly account for cluster-specific disadvantages. This indicates that improving cultural validity in creative thinking requires redesigning prompts and scoring guides to support multiple culturally legitimate routes to originality and appropriateness, rather than relying on statistical DIF detection alone.

data.outcome_summary: This open-access journal article analyzes cross-cultural differential item functioning in the OECD PISA 2022 Creative Thinking (CT) assessment for 15-year-olds, using secondary PISA 2022 international database microdata. The authors include 137,851 students from 63 participating countries/economies and calibrate an IRT-based DFIT framework across ten extended GLOBE cultural clusters, using the Anglo cluster as the reference group. Across 30 retained CT items, 83.3% were flagged for DIF above a practical threshold (NCDIF > 0.0115), with the largest effects reported for DT360Q01C2 (Max NCDIF = 0.188) and DT500Q01C (Max NCDIF = 0.176). Cluster-level aggregation shows systematic disadvantage for some clusters (e.g., Sub-Saharan Africa net mean SA = −0.690; DTF = 1.668) and net advantage for others (e.g., Confucian Asia net mean SA = 0.338; DTF = 3.944). The study does not report PV handling or a missing-data strategy for PVs because the DIF analysis is IRT-based on item responses; survey-weight use is also not explicitly documented, so population-representativeness of DIF indices should be interpreted cautiously.
